source: MIT 18.06 Linear Algebra, Lecture 1 (Gilbert Strang), ~20-28 min
keypoints: Each row of a 3x3 system gives a plane in three dimensions.
Two planes (the first two equations) meet in a line.
Three non-parallel, non-special planes meet in one point, and that point is the solution.
The row picture is easy for two lines but hard to visualize for three planes, and worse in higher dimensions.
The column picture of the 3x3 example is x(2,-1,0) + y(-1,2,-3) + z(0,-1,4) = (0,-1,4).
In this specially chosen example the right-hand side equals the third column, so the solution is (x, y, z) = (0, 0, 1).
The solution (0,0,1) is exactly the point where the three planes meet.
Elimination, covered next lecture, is the systematic method that all production large-scale software uses to solve systems in all cases.
The column picture asks: what combination of the three three-dimensional column vectors produces the right-hand side vector?
